Lecture 1 Lie groups and their tangent algebras

Self-checks · Read it in the lecture

  1. Why is GL⁡n(C)\GL_n(\C)GLn​(C) open in Cn2\C^{n^2}Cn2 but U⁡(n)\UU(n)U(n) is not?

  2. Does differentiating g(t)Tg(t)=Ig(t)^{\mathsf T}g(t)=Ig(t)Tg(t)=I prove that every skew-symmetric matrix is tangent to SO⁡(n)\SO(n)SO(n)?

  3. Is diag⁡(1,−1)\diag(1,-1)diag(1,−1) in su(2)\suu(2)su(2)? Is it in the complex span of su(2)\suu(2)su(2)?

Show the source answers

Answers. (1) The determinant is continuous, so the set where it is nonzero is open in Cn2\C^{n^2}Cn2. For real ε\varepsilonε with 0<∣ε∣<10<|\varepsilon|<10<∣ε∣<1, a unitary matrix UUU satisfies ((1+ε)U)∗((1+ε)U)=(1+ε)2I≠I.((1+\varepsilon)U)^*((1+\varepsilon)U)=(1+\varepsilon)^2I\ne I.((1+ε)U)∗((1+ε)U)=(1+ε)2I=I. These non-unitary matrices approach UUU, so no ambient ball about UUU lies in U⁡(n)\UU(n)U(n). (2) No. Differentiation proves necessity. The Cayley curve proves sufficiency. (3) No. The matrix diag⁡(1,−1)\diag(1,-1)diag(1,−1) is traceless but Hermitian, so it is not skew-Hermitian. It does lie in the complex span, since it equals −iA-iA−iA.

Show the complete source block, with its answers

  1. Which property of the Haar integral makes the form in the proof of unitarisability, Theorem 5.8, positive definite? Which makes it invariant?

    Answer. Strict positivity gives ⟨v,v⟩>0\langle v,v\rangle>0⟨v,v⟩>0 for v≠0v\ne0v=0. Right invariance gives invariance. Left invariance and normalisation enter only through the proof of strict positivity.

  2. Let Π\PiΠ be a nontrivial irreducible representation of a compact Lie group. What is ∫GΠ(g) dg\int_G\Pi(g)\,dg∫G​Π(g)dg?

    Answer. It is 000. By the invariant-vector projector, Proposition 5.10, its image is the subrepresentation VGV^GVG. Irreducibility gives VG=0V^G=0VG=0 or VG=VV^G=VVG=V. If VG=VV^G=VVG=V, then every Π(g)\Pi(g)Π(g) is the identity, so every line in VVV is invariant. Irreducibility then forces dim⁡V=1\dim V=1dimV=1, so Π\PiΠ is the trivial representation, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence VG=0V^G=0VG=0, and the integral is 000.

  3. Explain ∫SU⁡(2)a dg=0\int_{\SU(2)}a\,dg=0∫SU(2)​adg=0 in two ways.

    Answer. First, in Hopf coordinates the integrand carries the phase eiξ1e^{i\xi_1}eiξ1​, so the integral over ξ1\xi_1ξ1​ vanishes. Second, a=D11V1a=D^{V_1}_{11}a=D11V1​​, and the constant 111 is the matrix coefficient of the trivial representation V0V_0V0​. Since V1≇V0V_1\not\cong V_0V1​≅V0​, the relation for inequivalent representations in Corollary 5.13 gives ∫G1‾ a dg=0\int_G\overline{1}\,a\,dg=0∫G​1adg=0.

Show the complete source block, with its answers

1. Why is the operator (10.2) nonzero, although no invariant vector is known?

Answer. By the definition (10.2), ⟨u,Tu⟩=∫∣⟨Π(g)u,u⟩∣2 dg\langle u,Tu\rangle=\int|\langle\Pi(g)u,u\rangle|^2\,dg⟨u,Tu⟩=∫∣⟨Π(g)u,u⟩∣2dg. The integrand is continuous, nonnegative and equal to 111 at eee. By positivity (H2), the integral is positive. Hence TTT is nonzero.

1. Why must the stabiliser algebra contain the centre?

Answer. If XXX is central, then [X,Y]=0[X,Y]=0[X,Y]=0 for every YYY. The stabiliser formula (19.1) puts XXX in gℓ\g_\ellgℓ​ for every ℓ\ellℓ.

2. Does the formula ωλ=λ dp∧dq\omega_\lambda=\lambda\,dp\wedge dqωλ​=λdp∧dq have the right normalisation?

Answer. No. Its value on (−λ∂q,λ∂p)(-\lambda\partial_q,\lambda\partial_p)(−λ∂q​,λ∂p​) would be λ3\lambda^3λ3. The required value is λ\lambdaλ, so the coefficient is 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ.

3. Can one apply the orbit theorem directly to a Heisenberg group with circle centre?

Answer. No. That group is not simply connected. Apply the theorem to its simply connected cover. Then use the Descent theorem of Lecture 4. Only representations trivial on the covering kernel descend.

1. If r=3ℏ/2r=3\hbar/2r=3ℏ/2, find the normalised period and the quantised representation.

Answer. The period divided by 2πℏ2\pi\hbar2πℏ is 2r/ℏ=32r/\hbar=32r/ℏ=3. The bundle is O(3)\mathcal O(3)O(3) and its sections give V3V_3V3​, of dimension four and spin 3/23/23/2.

2. Does that sphere admit an SO⁡(3)\SO(3)SO(3)-equivariant prequantum lift with the orbit normalisation?

Answer. No. Its stabiliser character would be e3it/2e^{3it/2}e3it/2 on a rotation of period 2π2\pi2π. It takes the value −1-1−1 at t=2πt=2\pit=2π.

3. Why can the connection have local potentials although no global potential exists?

Answer. The difference of two local potentials is the logarithmic differential of a transition function. A nonzero curvature period prevents a single global primitive but is consistent with these local potentials.
